etymology: From Anglo-Saxon locc, a tress of hair. Webster 1828: a tuft or ringlet of hair. In the Nazarite law the uncut locks are the visible sign of a vow, and in Samson they became the most famous hair in Scripture.
biblical_def: The Nazarite vow had three marks — no wine, no contact with the dead, and no razor — and only the third could be seen: All the days of the vow of his separation there shall no razor come upon his head... he shall be holy, and shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow (Numbers 6:5). The hair is not the strength; it is the sign of the separation, which is why its loss mattered. Delilah works toward that sign by degrees: If thou weavest the seven locks of my head with the web (Judges 16:13), and Samson, playing with the secret, gives away its neighbourhood before he gives away the thing. Ezekiel legislates the priestly mean between two extremes: Neither shall they shave their heads, nor suffer their locks to grow long; they shall only poll their heads (Ezekiel 44:20) — neither the mourner’s shaven head nor the Nazarite’s long growth, but a trimmed and unremarkable ordinariness. And the Song uses the word for a lover kept waiting in the night: my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night (Song of Solomon 5:2).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LOCK, in this sense, as a tuft or ringlet of hair; a tress; and in the plural, the hair of the head collectively.
webster_full: LOCK, n. — A tuft of hair; a ringlet or tress.
In the plural, the hair of the head; as, hoary locks.
A tuft of wool or other fibrous substance.
Distinct from LOCK, an instrument to fasten a door, though the two words are spelled alike.
Anglo-Saxon locc, a lock of hair; compare German Locke.
scriptures: All the days of the vow of his separation there shall no razor come upon his head: until the days be fulfilled, in the which he separateth himself unto the LORD, he shall be holy, and shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow.
And Delilah said unto Samson, Hitherto thou hast mocked me, and told me lies: tell me wherewith thou mightest be bound. And he said unto her, If thou weavest the seven locks of my head with the web.
Neither shall they shave their heads, nor suffer their locks to grow long; they shall only poll their heads.

I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh, saying, Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled: for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night.
corruption_summary: Samson’s hair is popularly treated as a magic charm, which misses the point of the narrative: the hair was a sign of consecration, and what he lost was the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: The retelling that makes Samson’s strength reside in his hair turns a covenant narrative into a folk tale, and Judges is careful to prevent it. When the locks are cut the text does not say his strength departed but something far graver: he wist not that the LORD was departed from him (Judges 16:20). The strength was never in the hair; the hair was the visible token of a separation to God, and the LORD who gave the strength withdrew when the vow was finally discarded. Note also the manner of the loss — not a single betrayal but a sequence of games with the secret, each one closer, until the thing itself was surrendered to a lap. That is how consecration is usually lost, and it is why the sign mattered: a visible mark makes a private erosion harder to hide.

Ezekiel 44:20 is worth setting alongside, because it legislates against both extremes and the balance is instructive. Priests were forbidden the shaven head (the mourner’s and the pagan’s sign) and forbidden long-grown locks (the Nazarite’s sign); they were to poll their heads — trimmed, ordinary, unremarkable. God’s ministers were not to be identifiable by a striking appearance in either direction. There is a standing application in that for those who serve the church, and it cuts against the instinct to mark out spiritual seriousness by conspicuous difference. The Reformers made a related point against clerical costume and tonsure: the minister is a man among men, distinguished by office and doctrine rather than by hair.
roots_summary: Hebrew pera (H6545), long hair, the loose locks of a Nazarite; machlaphah (H4253), a braid or plait; nazir (H5139), one separated, a Nazarite.
roots_lines: Hebrew pera (H6545) — the loose or long hair of the head; the locks of the hair of his head (Numbers 6:5) and the forbidden growth of Ezekiel 44:20.
Hebrew machlaphah (H4253) — a braid or plait; the seven locks of my head (Judges 16:13).
Hebrew nazir (H5139) — one separated or consecrated; the Nazarite whose uncut hair is the sign.
Hebrew taar (H8593) — a razor; the instrument forbidden all the days of the vow.
Hebrew kasam (H3697) — to shear or poll; the priestly trimming commanded in Ezekiel 44:20.
usage: He shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow (Numbers 6:5) — the one mark of the vow that could be seen.
If thou weavest the seven locks of my head with the web (Judges 16:13) — the secret given away by degrees.
Neither shall they shave their heads, nor suffer their locks to grow long (Ezekiel 44:20) — the priestly mean between two conspicuous extremes.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon toth. Webster 1828: a bony substance growing out of the jaws. In the law it names the principle of exact and limited retribution, and our Lord addresses it directly in the Sermon on the Mount.
biblical_def: Tooth for tooth is the shorthand for the lex talionis, the law of exact recompense: Eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot (Exodus 21:24), repeated in Leviticus with the governing principle stated: as he hath caused a blemish in a man, so shall it be done to him again (Leviticus 24:20). The purpose of the rule is limitation. In a world where an injury invited a family’s vengeance, the law fixed the maximum at the exact equivalent and put its execution in the hands of judges rather than the injured. Our Lord quotes it and then addresses what His hearers had made of it: Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth (Matthew 5:38) — and the following verses forbid the disciple to take private retaliation at all. Proverbs uses the word for a different kind of failure: Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint (Proverbs 25:19) — things that fail precisely at the moment of pressure.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TOOTH as a bony substance growing out of the jaws of animals, serving to bite and chew; and figuratively, taste, palate, or a sharp prominence.
webster_full: TOOTH, n. (pl. TEETH) — A bony substance growing out of the jaws, and serving as the instrument of mastication.
Taste; palate; as, a sweet tooth.
A prominence or sharp projection; as the tooth of a saw or comb.
TOOTH AND NAIL, with one’s utmost power; by all possible means.
Anglo-Saxon toth; compare Latin dens, Greek odous.
scriptures: Eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,
Breach for breach, eye for eye, tooth for tooth: as he hath caused a blemish in a man, so shall it be done to him again.
Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth:
Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint.
corruption_summary: The lex talionis is popularly cited as evidence of Old Testament savagery, when it was a limitation on vengeance and a judicial standard, not a licence for private revenge.
corruption_paragraphs: Eye for eye, tooth for tooth is one of the most misquoted principles in Scripture. Read against its ancient setting, where an injury commonly provoked escalating blood feud — Lamech in Genesis 4:24 boasting of seventy-sevenfold vengeance — the rule is a ceiling rather than a floor. It says the penalty may not exceed the injury, and Deuteronomy 19:18-21 places its administration with the judges, not the aggrieved. Far from primitive cruelty, it is the origin in Western law of proportionality in sentencing. The habit of contrasting a vengeful Old Testament God with a merciful New Testament Christ founders here as elsewhere: the same God gave both, and Christ Himself affirms that He came not to destroy the law but to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17).

What our Lord addresses in Matthew 5:38 is the private use of a judicial rule. His hearers had taken a standard given to courts and made it a warrant for personal retaliation, and He forbids the disciple that ground entirely — turn the other cheek, go the second mile. This does not abolish the magistrate’s sword; Romans 13:4 keeps it, and the same Christ will judge the world. The Reformed distinction between the spheres is what holds the two together: the individual Christian renounces private vengeance, while public justice remains God’s ordinance administered through the magistrate. Pacifist readings collapse the distinction one way; the appeal to Exodus 21 as a personal right collapses it the other.
roots_summary: Hebrew shen (H8127), a tooth; mum (H3971), a blemish; Greek odous (G3599), a tooth; the phrase lex talionis, the law of like for like.
roots_lines: Hebrew shen (H8127) — a tooth; the second term of the formula in Exodus 21:24 and Leviticus 24:20.
Hebrew mum (H3971) — a blemish or defect; the governing principle of Leviticus 24:20.
Greek odous (G3599) — a tooth; our Lord’s quotation in Matthew 5:38.
Hebrew shabar (H7665) — to break; the broken tooth of Proverbs 25:19.
Hebrew bagad (H898) — to deal treacherously; the unfaithful man whose confidence fails (Proverbs 25:19).
usage: Eye for eye, tooth for tooth (Exodus 21:24) — a ceiling on vengeance, not a floor.
As he hath caused a blemish in a man, so shall it be done to him again (Leviticus 24:20) — exactness is the whole point.
Like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint (Proverbs 25:19) — things that fail precisely under pressure.

etymology: From Latin solea, a sandal or the bottom of the foot, from solum, the ground. Webster 1828: the bottom of the foot; the bottom of a shoe. Scripture uses it to mark the smallest possible measure of rest and the largest possible grant of territory.
biblical_def: The word measures the least amount of ground a creature needs, and Genesis uses it to say the flood had left none: the dove found no rest for the sole of her foot, and she returned unto him into the ark, for the waters were on the face of the whole earth (Genesis 8:9). The same figure becomes a covenant curse for a scattered people: among these nations shalt thou find no ease, neither shall the sole of thy foot have rest: but the LORD shall give thee there a trembling heart (Deuteronomy 28:65). Against these Joshua receives the promise in the opposite direction, where the sole of the foot measures possession rather than homelessness: Every place that the sole of your foot shall tread upon, that have I given unto you, as I said unto Moses (Joshua 1:3). The grant is real and it is entered by walking. Isaiah uses the phrase to sweep a whole body in one clause and finds nothing sound in it: From the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it; but wounds, and bruises, and putrifying sores (Isaiah 1:6).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SOLE as the bottom of the foot; and hence the bottom of a shoe, or the piece of leather which constitutes it; the foot itself.
webster_full: SOLE, n. — The bottom of the foot; and by a figure, the foot itself.
The bottom of a shoe; or the piece of leather which constitutes the bottom.
The part of anything that forms its lower surface; as the sole of a plough.
SOLE, a. — Single; only; being or acting without another. (A distinct word, from Latin solus.)
Latin solea, a sandal, from solum, the ground or bottom.
scriptures: But the dove found no rest for the sole of her foot, and she returned unto him into the ark, for the waters were on the face of the whole earth: then he put forth his hand, and took her, and pulled her in unto him into the ark.
And among these nations shalt thou find no ease, neither shall the sole of thy foot have rest: but the LORD shall give thee there a trembling heart, and failing of eyes, and sorrow of mind:
Every place that the sole of your foot shall tread upon, that have I given unto you, as I said unto Moses.
From the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it; but wounds, and bruises, and putrifying sores: they have not been closed, neither bound up, neither mollified with ointment.
corruption_summary: Joshua 1:3 is a land grant to Israel under a specific covenant, and its routine use as a personal promise of territorial expansion detaches it from everything the chapter says.
corruption_paragraphs: Every place that the sole of your foot shall tread upon, that have I given unto you is spoken to Joshua, about Canaan, with boundaries specified in the next verse, in fulfilment of a promise made to Moses. Its modern career as a personal warrant for claiming ground — territory, influence, markets — requires ignoring the boundaries, the covenant, and the addressee. The chapter’s own emphasis is the opposite of expansionist: what Joshua is told three times is to be strong and of a good courage, and the means given him is the book of the law, which he is to meditate in day and night that he may observe to do according to all that is written therein (Joshua 1:8). The promise is inseparable from the obedience it is attached to, and the possession is of a particular land God had named.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the way Scripture measures by the smallest unit. The dove could not find a foot’s width of rest; the scattered nation would not find a foot’s width of ease; Isaiah’s patient has no soundness in a single inch from sole to head. This is how the Bible states totality — not by abstraction but by naming the least part and denying it. The doctrine of total depravity is often heard as a claim that men are as bad as they could possibly be, which it does not mean; Isaiah 1:6 shows the actual sense, which is extent rather than degree. There is no part of the man — mind, will, affections, body — that the fall left untouched.
roots_summary: Hebrew kaph (H3709), the palm or hollow, used of the sole of the foot; regel (H7272), the foot; manoach (H4494), a resting place.
roots_lines: Hebrew kaph regel — the hollow of the foot, the sole; the phrase in Genesis 8:9, Deuteronomy 28:65 and Joshua 1:3.
Hebrew manoach (H4494) — a resting place; what the dove could not find (Genesis 8:9).
Hebrew darak (H1869) — to tread or march; the sole of your foot shall tread upon (Joshua 1:3).
Hebrew methom (H4974) — soundness, wholeness; what Isaiah finds nowhere in the body (Isaiah 1:6).
Hebrew ragaz (H7264) — to tremble or quiver; the trembling heart of the covenant curse (Deuteronomy 28:65).
usage: The dove found no rest for the sole of her foot (Genesis 8:9) — the least measure of ground, and there was none.
Every place that the sole of your foot shall tread upon, that have I given unto you (Joshua 1:3) — a real grant, entered by walking.
From the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it (Isaiah 1:6) — totality stated by naming the least part.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon scafan, to scrape or pare. Webster 1828: to cut or pare off something from the surface by a razor. In Scripture shaving is almost always ritual or judicial — a sign of cleansing, of mourning, of humiliation, or of a vow interrupted.
biblical_def: Shaving in Israel was rarely cosmetic. The Nazarite whose vow was defiled by a sudden death must begin again, and the razor marks the interruption: he hath defiled the head of his consecration; then he shall shave his head in the day of his cleansing, on the seventh day shall he shave it (Numbers 6:9). The cleansed leper shaves; so does the captive woman a man would marry, whose old life is deliberately put off: thou shalt bring her home to thine house; and she shall shave her head, and pare her nails (Deuteronomy 21:12) — a law which, whatever else it does, forbids the treatment of a captive as spoil and requires a full month before marriage. Isaiah turns shaving into a figure of national humiliation with a razor God has hired: In the same day shall the Lord shave with a razor that is hired, namely, by them beyond the river, by the king of Assyria, the head, and the hair of the feet: and it shall also consume the beard (Isaiah 7:20). Paul appeals to the same sense of disgrace in his argument about covering: if it be a shame for a woman to be shorn or shaven, let her be covered (1 Corinthians 11:6).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SHAVE as to cut or pare off something from the surface of a body by a razor or other edged instrument; to cut off the hair from the skin.
webster_full: SHAVE, v.t. — To cut or pare off something from the surface of a body by a razor or other edged instrument.
To cut off the hair from the skin with a razor; as, to shave the head.
To skim along the surface near to; to sweep along.
To strip; to oppress by extortion; to fleece.
Anglo-Saxon scafan, to scrape or shave; compare shape and scab.
scriptures: And if any man die very suddenly by him, and he hath defiled the head of his consecration; then he shall shave his head in the day of his cleansing, on the seventh day shall he shave it.
Then thou shalt bring her home to thine house; and she shall shave her head, and pare her nails;
In the same day shall the Lord shave with a razor that is hired, namely, by them beyond the river, by the king of Assyria, the head, and the hair of the feet: and it shall also consume the beard.
For if the woman be not covered, let her also be shorn: but if it be a shame for a woman to be shorn or shaven, let her be covered.
corruption_summary: Deuteronomy 21:10-14 is regularly cited as evidence that Scripture licenses the taking of captive women, when the law it states is a restraint that forbids exactly that treatment.
corruption_paragraphs: The passage is a favourite of the popular case against the Old Testament, and its actual provisions run the other way. A captive woman may not be used; she is brought into the house, her head shaved and nails pared, her captive’s clothing removed, and she bewails her father and mother a full month — and only then may she be married, as a wife with a wife’s standing. If the man has no delight in her she must be let go free, and the law states the reason plainly: thou shalt not sell her at all for money, thou shalt not make merchandise of her, because thou hast humbled her (Deuteronomy 21:14). In an ancient world where captive women were property, this legislation interposes a month of mourning, a formal marriage, and a prohibition on sale. The Mosaic case laws regulate a fallen world without endorsing it, and reading a restraint as a permission inverts the text.

1 Corinthians 11:6 rests on a cultural fact — that a shorn or shaven head was a disgrace to a woman in Corinth — and builds on a creational argument that is not cultural: the order of headship in verse 3, which runs God, Christ, man, woman, and which Paul grounds in the account of creation. Two errors follow from missing the distinction. The first treats the whole passage as time-bound and discards the order along with the head-covering; the second absolutizes the local sign and makes a first-century Corinthian custom a permanent ordinance. This dictionary holds the creational order that Paul argues from, while recognising that the sign by which it was expressed in Corinth was a sign, and that Paul himself ends the passage by appealing to the custom of the churches.
roots_summary: Hebrew galach (H1548), to shave or make bald; taar (H8593), a razor; Greek xurao (G3587), to shave; keiro (G2751), to shear.
roots_lines: Hebrew galach (H1548) — to shave, to make bald; used of the Nazarite (Numbers 6:9) and the captive woman (Deuteronomy 21:12).
Hebrew taar (H8593) — a razor; the hired razor of Isaiah 7:20, which is Assyria.
Greek xurao (G3587) — to shave with a razor; shorn or shaven (1 Corinthians 11:6).
Greek keiro (G2751) — to shear or cut short, as a sheep; the companion verb in the same verse.
Hebrew nezer (H5145) — consecration, separation; the head of his consecration (Numbers 6:9).
usage: He shall shave his head in the day of his cleansing (Numbers 6:9) — a vow defiled must begin again.
She shall shave her head, and pare her nails (Deuteronomy 21:12) — a law of restraint, not of licence.
The Lord shall shave with a razor that is hired (Isaiah 7:20) — Assyria as God’s hired instrument of humiliation.

etymology: From Middle English balled, having a white patch, of uncertain origin. Webster 1828: destitute of hair, particularly on the top or back of the head. The law declares the bald man clean, and Israel’s enemies make themselves bald in mourning.
biblical_def: Leviticus 13, which legislates at length about skin disease, pauses to make an explicit exemption: the man whose hair is fallen off his head, he is bald; yet is he clean (Leviticus 13:40). Ordinary baldness carries no ceremonial defilement, and the verse exists to prevent a priest from treating a natural condition as a plague. Deliberate baldness is another matter: it was a pagan mourning rite, and the prophets describe it as the mark of overwhelming grief. Jeremiah on Moab: every head shall be bald, and every beard clipped: upon all the hands shall be cuttings, and upon the loins sackcloth (Jeremiah 48:37). Ezekiel on the lament for Tyre: they shall make themselves utterly bald for thee, and gird them with sackcloth, and they shall weep for thee with bitterness of heart and bitter wailing (Ezekiel 27:31). And the word supplies the taunt flung at Elisha as he went up to Bethel: there came forth little children out of the city, and mocked him, and said unto him, Go up, thou bald head; go up, thou bald head (2 Kings 2:23).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BALD as destitute of hair, especially on the top and back of the head; and figuratively, destitute of ornament, unadorned, inelegant.
webster_full: BALD, a. — Destitute of hair, especially on the top and back of the head.
Destitute of the natural covering; as a bald oak.
Without ornament; unadorned; inelegant; as a bald style.
Bare; naked; open; undisguised; as the bald truth.
Middle English balled, marked with a white patch; compare the bald eagle, so called from its white head.
scriptures: And the man whose hair is fallen off his head, he is bald; yet is he clean.
For every head shall be bald, and every beard clipped: upon all the hands shall be cuttings, and upon the loins sackcloth.
And they shall make themselves utterly bald for thee, and gird them with sackcloth, and they shall weep for thee with bitterness of heart and bitter wailing.

And he went up from thence unto Bethel: and as he was going up by the way, there came forth little children out of the city, and mocked him, and said unto him, Go up, thou bald head; go up, thou bald head.
corruption_summary: The mocking of Elisha at Bethel is a favourite text for the charge that the God of the Old Testament is capricious, and the objection rests on a mistranslation of the mockers’ age and a misreading of what they said.
corruption_paragraphs: The scene is regularly presented as small children teasing a bald man and being killed by bears for it. The Hebrew nearim covers a wide range and is used elsewhere of young men of military age; Joseph is called a naar at seventeen. More decisive is what they said. Go up, thou bald head is not a comment on hair alone: Elijah had just gone up in a whirlwind, and Bethel was the seat of Jeroboam’s calf worship. A crowd of young men from the apostate cult centre, telling the LORD’s newly commissioned prophet to go up as his master had, are not mocking an appearance but repudiating a succession. The judgment falls on Bethel’s contempt for the prophetic word, and the narrative sits within a long account of that city’s idolatry. This does not make the passage comfortable, and Scripture does not offer it as comfortable; it offers it as a warning about despising God’s messengers.

Leviticus 13:40 deserves notice for what it prevents. In a chapter devoted to identifying defiling skin conditions, the lawgiver stops to say that ordinary hair loss is clean, and repeats the exemption for forehead baldness in the next verse. God’s law protects men from over-scrupulous priests as well as from real defilement, and the pastoral instinct behind that is worth naming: a system of holiness can be made cruel by those who apply it beyond its terms, and the law itself forecloses the abuse. The Pharisees of the Gospels are condemned for precisely the opposite habit, binding heavy burdens that Moses never laid on anyone.
roots_summary: Hebrew qereach (H7142), bald, bald-headed; qorchah (H7144), baldness, a bald spot; gabbach (H1371), bald in the forehead.
roots_lines: Hebrew qereach (H7142) — bald on the back of the head; he is bald; yet is he clean (Leviticus 13:40) and the taunt at Bethel (2 Kings 2:23).
Hebrew qorchah (H7144) — baldness made as a sign of mourning; forbidden to Israel in Deuteronomy 14:1.
Hebrew gabbach (H1371) — bald in the forehead; the companion exemption of Leviticus 13:41.
Hebrew naar (H5288) — a young man or lad, a wide term used of Joseph at seventeen; the mockers of 2 Kings 2:23.
Hebrew saq (H8242) — sackcloth, the mourning garment joined to baldness in Jeremiah 48:37 and Ezekiel 27:31.
usage: He is bald; yet is he clean (Leviticus 13:40) — the law forestalling an over-scrupulous priest.
Every head shall be bald, and every beard clipped (Jeremiah 48:37) — deliberate baldness as the mark of overwhelming grief.
Go up, thou bald head (2 Kings 2:23) — not a comment on hair but a repudiation of a prophetic succession.

etymology: Plural of fly, from Anglo-Saxon fleoge. Webster 1828: a small winged insect. The fourth plague of Egypt was swarms of them, and Ecclesiastes makes a dead fly the figure for a small folly in a great reputation.
biblical_def: The fourth plague is announced in terms that stress penetration rather than mere nuisance: I will send swarms of flies upon thee, and upon thy servants, and upon thy people, and into thy houses: and the houses of the Egyptians shall be full of swarms of flies (Exodus 8:21). The plague reaches into the houses, and the following verses record the first explicit separation of Goshen — Israel’s land is exempted, so that Pharaoh may know that the LORD is in the midst of the earth. Asaph recalls it in his rehearsal of the exodus: He sent divers sorts of flies among them, which devoured them; and frogs, which destroyed them (Psalm 78:45). Ecclesiastes turns the insect into one of the most quoted proverbs about reputation: Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour (Ecclesiastes 10:1). A very small corruption spoils a very costly thing. And Isaiah makes the fly an image of summoned armies: the LORD shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria (Isaiah 7:18).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FLY as a small winged insect of numerous species, particularly the common house-fly; and notes its proverbial use for something small that corrupts or annoys out of all proportion to its size.
webster_full: FLY, n. (pl. FLIES) — A small winged insect of many species, particularly the house-fly.
In Scripture, swarms of insects sent as a plague upon Egypt.
Anything small and troublesome out of proportion to its size.
FLY-BLOWN, a. — Tainted with the eggs of flies; corrupted.
Anglo-Saxon fleoge, from fleogan, to fly.
scriptures: Else, if thou wilt not let my people go, behold, I will send swarms of flies upon thee, and upon thy servants, and upon thy people, and into thy houses: and the houses of the Egyptians shall be full of swarms of flies, and also the ground whereon they are.
He sent divers sorts of flies among them, which devoured them; and frogs, which destroyed them.
Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour.
And it shall come to pass in that day, that the LORD shall hiss for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria.
corruption_summary: Ecclesiastes 10:1 says a little folly ruins a great reputation, which the modern instinct to treat character failures in leaders as separable from their gifts flatly denies.
corruption_paragraphs: Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom and honour. The proverb is about proportion. The ointment is costly and carefully compounded; the fly is small and dead; and the result is not a slightly diminished perfume but a stink. Applied to leadership, it contradicts the settled modern habit of separating a man’s gifts from his character — of arguing that the teaching stands whatever the teacher did. Scripture does not permit that division: the qualifications for elder in 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 are almost entirely about character, with apt to teach the single exception. A ministry is not a product that can be assessed apart from the man, and the reason is stated here in a sentence about ointment.

The plagues are worth naming as history rather than symbol. Exodus presents them as a judicial contest with the gods of Egypt (Exodus 12:12), announced in advance, escalating, and marked from the fourth onward by the explicit exemption of Goshen so that Pharaoh might know the LORD is in the midst of the earth. The critical reading that reduces them to a folk memory of natural disasters, or to a late literary construction, has to account for a narrative whose whole point is discrimination — flies here and not there, at a time announced beforehand. This dictionary holds Mosaic authorship and the historicity of the exodus, and the plague narratives are not decoration on that claim; they are the demonstration the text says they were.
roots_summary: Hebrew arob (H6157), a swarm, the mixture of insects of the fourth plague; zebub (H2070), a fly; Greek Beelzeboul (G954), lord of flies, from the Philistine god of Ekron.
roots_lines: Hebrew arob (H6157) — a swarm or mixture of insects; the fourth plague (Exodus 8:21; Psalm 78:45).
Hebrew zebub (H2070) — a fly; dead flies in Ecclesiastes 10:1.
Hebrew Baal-zebub (H1176) — lord of the fly, the god of Ekron consulted by Ahaziah (2 Kings 1:2).
Greek Beelzeboul (G954) — the New Testament form, applied to the prince of the devils (Matthew 12:24).
Hebrew sharaq (H8319) — to hiss or whistle; the LORD summoning the fly and the bee (Isaiah 7:18).
usage: I will send swarms of flies... into your houses (Exodus 8:21) — the plague reaches indoors, and Goshen is exempted.
Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour (Ecclesiastes 10:1) — a small corruption spoiling a costly thing.
The LORD shall hiss for the fly... and for the bee (Isaiah 7:18) — armies summoned like insects.

etymology: From foot and men: soldiers who serve on foot, as distinguished from cavalry; also, runners or attendants. Webster 1828: soldiers who march and fight on foot. Jeremiah uses them as the measure of the easier trial.
biblical_def: The LORD’s answer to Jeremiah’s complaint is not comfort but a question, and it is one of the most bracing verses in the prophets: If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? and if in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee, then how wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan? (Jeremiah 12:5). Jeremiah had asked why the wicked prosper; God replies that harder things are coming and that the present trouble is the lesser race. The word is a military one, denoting infantry as against cavalry. Moses uses it to count the nation: The people, among whom I am, are six hundred thousand footmen; and thou hast said, I will give them flesh, that they may eat a whole month (Numbers 11:21) — the arithmetic of unbelief, offered to God as an objection. And in one of the darkest scenes in Samuel, the king’s footmen refuse an order: the king said unto the footmen that stood about him, Turn, and slay the priests of the LORD... But the servants of the king would not put forth their hand to fall upon the priests of the LORD (1 Samuel 22:17).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FOOTMAN as a soldier who marches and fights on foot; also a runner, or a menial servant who attends on foot; in the plural, infantry.
webster_full: FOOTMAN, n. (pl. FOOTMEN) — A soldier who marches and fights on foot.
A runner; one who attends on foot.
A menial servant; a male attendant.
In the plural, infantry, as distinguished from horsemen or cavalry.
From foot and man.
scriptures: If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? and if in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee, then how wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan?
And Moses said, The people, among whom I am, are six hundred thousand footmen; and thou hast said, I will give them flesh, that they may eat a whole month.

And the king said unto the footmen that stood about him, Turn, and slay the priests of the LORD; because their hand also is with David, and because they knew when he fled, and did not shew it to me. But the servants of the king would not put forth their hand to fall upon the priests of the LORD.

Righteous art thou, O LORD, when I plead with thee: yet let me talk with thee of thy judgments: Wherefore doth the way of the wicked prosper? wherefore are all they happy that deal very treacherously?
corruption_summary: God’s reply to Jeremiah’s complaint is not consolation but a warning of harder trials, which contradicts the pastoral assumption that God’s answer to a struggling servant is always relief.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah asks the oldest question — why the wicked prosper — and receives an answer no modern pastoral manual would recommend: If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? God does not explain the prosperity of the wicked, does not promise relief, and does not soften the coming difficulty. He tells His prophet that this was the easy part. The therapeutic assumption that a struggling believer must first be reassured cannot accommodate the verse, and it is worth noticing that Jeremiah was not thereby crushed: he went on to a ministry of forty years and to the book of Lamentations. God’s honesty about what was coming was itself a mercy, and preparing a servant is a different kind of kindness from comforting him.

1 Samuel 22:17 records one of Scripture’s clearest instances of lawful disobedience to a superior. Saul, the anointed king, commands his footmen to kill the priests of the LORD, and they refuse — and the narrative does not censure them. It was Doeg the Edomite who obeyed, and eighty-five priests died. The episode establishes what Romans 13 assumes and Acts 5:29 states: obedience to authority is owed within the bounds of God’s law and stops where a magistrate commands sin. The footmen had no office and no standing; they simply would not put forth their hand. The Reformed doctrine of the lesser magistrate develops the case of resistance through subordinate authority, but this passage shows the simpler duty that lies beneath it, which belongs to any man asked to do murder.
roots_summary: Hebrew ragli (H7273), one on foot, a footman; ruts (H7323), to run; parash (H6571), a horseman; the contrast in Jeremiah 12:5 is between infantry and cavalry.
roots_lines: Hebrew ragli (H7273) — on foot, a footman; from regel, the foot (Jeremiah 12:5; Numbers 11:21).
Hebrew ruts (H7323) — to run; if thou hast run with the footmen (Jeremiah 12:5).
Hebrew sus (H5483) — a horse; the harder contest of the same verse.
Hebrew gaon (H1347) — swelling, majesty, pride; the swelling of Jordan, the flooded thickets where lions lodged.
Hebrew ruts in 1 Samuel 22:17 — the king’s runners or guard, rendered footmen.
usage: If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee (Jeremiah 12:5) — God tells His prophet this was the easy part.
Six hundred thousand footmen (Numbers 11:21) — the arithmetic of unbelief, offered to God as an objection.
The servants of the king would not put forth their hand (1 Samuel 22:17) — lawful refusal of an unlawful command.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon staeger, from stigan, to climb or ascend. Webster 1828: a series of steps by which persons ascend to a higher room. In Scripture the stairs are where a man stands to be seen and heard, and where a dove hides.
biblical_def: Solomon’s temple had a concealed ascent: The door for the middle chamber was in the right side of the house: and they went up with winding stairs into the middle chamber, and out of the middle into the third (1 Kings 6:8). The side chambers rose in three storeys and the stair turned inside the wall, unseen from the court. Nehemiah records the rebuilding of another set: the wall of the pool of Siloah by the king's garden, and unto the stairs that go down from the city of David (Nehemiah 3:15) — ordinary masonry named in a chapter that is a roll of honour for people who repaired what was in front of their own houses. In the New Testament the stairs of the Antonia fortress become a pulpit: when he had given him licence, Paul stood on the stairs, and beckoned with the hand unto the people. And when there was made a great silence, he spake unto them in the Hebrew tongue (Acts 21:40) — a prisoner between a mob and a Roman garrison, preaching in the mob’s own language. And the Song places the beloved in the hidden turn of a stair: O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance (Song of Solomon 2:14).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines STAIR as a step; one of a series of steps by which persons ascend to a higher room or level; and in the plural, a flight of such steps.
webster_full: STAIR, n. — A step; a stone or a frame of boards or planks by which a person rises one step.
In the plural, STAIRS, a flight of steps by which persons ascend to a higher room or story.
WINDING STAIRS, a flight of steps turning about a newel or centre.
STAIRCASE, n. — The part of a building which contains the stairs.
Anglo-Saxon staeger, from stigan, to ascend — the root of sty and stile.
scriptures: The door for the middle chamber was in the right side of the house: and they went up with winding stairs into the middle chamber, and out of the middle into the third.

But the gate of the fountain repaired Shallun the son of Colhozeh, the ruler of part of Mizpah; he built it, and covered it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof, and the wall of the pool of Siloah by the king's garden, and unto the stairs that go down from the city of David.
And when he had given him licence, Paul stood on the stairs, and beckoned with the hand unto the people. And when there was made a great silence, he spake unto them in the Hebrew tongue, saying,
O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.
corruption_summary: Nehemiah 3 is a chapter of names and masonry that modern reading skips, and it contains the plainest biblical picture of ordinary people repairing what lies in front of their own door.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of unremarkable work. Nehemiah 3 lists goldsmiths, apothecaries, merchants and rulers, each repairing a named section — and repeatedly, over against his house. The chapter also records that the nobles of Tekoa put not their necks to the work of their Lord (Nehemiah 3:5), which is the only censure in the list and falls on the men best able to help. Stairs, doors, locks and bars are named individually. A church culture that measures usefulness by visibility has no category for this chapter, and would not have written it down. Scripture keeps the record, which is itself the doctrine: God notices the section of wall in front of a man’s own house.

Acts 21:40 is worth pausing over for what Paul does with a moment of extremity. He has been dragged from the temple, beaten, and rescued by a Roman commander who assumed he was an Egyptian revolutionary. Standing in chains on the fortress stairs, with licence granted to speak, he addresses the crowd in Hebrew and gives them his testimony. He does not defend his liberty, protest his treatment, or address the Romans who held him; he preaches to the people who had just tried to kill him, in their own tongue, and the change of language alone quiets them. That is the apostolic instinct about a platform: it is for the gospel, and the audience is the one that needs it most.
roots_summary: Hebrew maalah (H4609), a step or ascent, the word also used of the Songs of Degrees; lul (H3883), a winding stair; Greek anabathmos (G304), a flight of steps.
roots_lines: Hebrew lul (H3883) — a spiral or winding stair; the concealed ascent of Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 6:8).
Hebrew maalah (H4609) — a step, stair, or ascent; also the title-word of the Psalms of Degrees.
Greek anabathmos (G304) — a flight of steps; the stairs of the Antonia fortress (Acts 21:40).
Hebrew madregah (H4095) — a steep place or stair; the secret places of the stairs (Song of Solomon 2:14).
Greek Hebrais dialektos — the Hebrew tongue, the language that quieted the crowd (Acts 21:40).
usage: They went up with winding stairs into the middle chamber (1 Kings 6:8) — an ascent turning inside the wall, unseen from the court.
Unto the stairs that go down from the city of David (Nehemiah 3:15) — masonry named in a roll of honour.
Paul stood on the stairs, and beckoned with the hand unto the people (Acts 21:40) — a prisoner preaching in the mob’s own language.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon hol, a hollow place, a cavern. Webster 1828: a hollow place or cavity in any solid body; an opening. Isaiah tells a people to look back at the pit they were dug from, and the reason he gives is comfort.
biblical_def: Isaiah addresses people already seeking the LORD and tells them to look backward, not for shame but for encouragement: Hearken to me, ye that follow after righteousness, ye that seek the LORD: look unto the rock whence ye are hewn, and to the hole of the pit whence ye are digged (Isaiah 51:1). The next verse names the rock and the pit — Abraham and Sarah, called when he was one and childless. The argument is that God multiplied from a single barren couple, and will do so again. The word also names a small and homely mechanism of temple reform: Jehoiada the priest took a chest, and bored a hole in the lid of it, and set it beside the altar (2 Kings 12:9) — the first collection box in Scripture, introduced because money given for repairs had not been reaching the repairs. Isaiah uses the word again for the peace of the coming kingdom, where the deadliest thing in a child’s world is harmless: the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice' den (Isaiah 11:8). And the Song has the beloved reach through: My beloved put in his hand by the hole of the door, and my bowels were moved for him (Song of Solomon 5:4).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HOLE as a hollow place or cavity in any solid body; an opening or perforation; a cave or den; a mean habitation.
webster_full: HOLE, n. — A hollow place or cavity in any solid body, of any shape or dimensions.
An opening or perforation; as a hole in a garment.
A cave; a den; a hollow place in the earth; the retreat of a beast.
A mean habitation; a narrow or dark lodging.
Anglo-Saxon hol, a hollow; connected with hollow and hell in its older sense of a covered place.
scriptures: Hearken to me, ye that follow after righteousness, ye that seek the LORD: look unto the rock whence ye are hewn, and to the hole of the pit whence ye are digged.

But Jehoiada the priest took a chest, and bored a hole in the lid of it, and set it beside the altar, on the right side as one cometh into the house of the LORD: and the priests that kept the door put therein all the money that was brought into the house of the LORD.
And the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice' den.
Look unto Abraham your father, and unto Sarah that bare you: for I called him alone, and blessed him, and increased him.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 51:1-2 tells believers to remember what they were dug from, and the remembering is offered as comfort rather than as shame — an order the therapeutic and the moralistic both get wrong.
corruption_paragraphs: Look unto the rock whence ye are hewn, and to the hole of the pit whence ye are digged — and the next verse identifies them: Abraham, called alone, and Sarah, who bore. The recollection is meant to encourage a small and discouraged remnant by reminding them that God has built a nation out of less than they currently have. Two habits get this wrong. The moralistic use makes the pit a rebuke, a reminder of unworthiness deployed to keep a believer humbled; Isaiah uses it to raise their hopes. The therapeutic instinct avoids the pit altogether, on the ground that dwelling on origins is unhelpful; Isaiah commands the looking. Paul does the same in 1 Corinthians 6:11 — such were some of you — and in Ephesians 2:11-13, where remembering what they were is the ground of wonder at what they are.

2 Kings 12:9 is an unexpectedly practical text. Money given for the repair of the house of the LORD had been collected for years and the breaches were not being mended, so Jehoiada bored a hole in a chest lid and set it by the altar, and 2 Kings 12:15 records that no reckoning was required of the men who handled it, for they dealt faithfully. Both halves are instructive: the structure was changed so that giving reached its object, and the men who then handled it were trustworthy enough that auditing was unnecessary. Scripture’s pattern for church finance is neither naive nor suspicious — Paul arranged for the collection to be carried by chosen representatives, providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men (2 Corinthians 8:21).
roots_summary: Hebrew maqqebeth (H4718), a hole or excavation; chor (H2356), a hole or cavity; bor (H953), a pit or cistern; gur (H4631), a den.
roots_lines: Hebrew maqqebeth (H4718) — an excavation or quarry-hole; the hole of the pit whence ye are digged (Isaiah 51:1).
Hebrew bor (H953) — a pit, well or cistern, often hewn from rock; the pit of the same verse.
Hebrew chor (H2356) — a hole or aperture; the hole of the asp (Isaiah 11:8) and the hole of the door (Song of Solomon 5:4).
Hebrew naqab (H5344) — to bore or pierce; Jehoiada boring the chest lid (2 Kings 12:9).
Hebrew pethen (H6620) — the asp or cobra; the creature made harmless in Isaiah 11:8.
usage: Look... to the hole of the pit whence ye are digged (Isaiah 51:1) — the remembering is comfort, not rebuke.
Bored a hole in the lid of it, and set it beside the altar (2 Kings 12:9) — the first collection box, and the reason it was needed.
The sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp (Isaiah 11:8) — the deadliest thing in a child’s world made harmless.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon nosu. Webster 1828: the prominent part of the face which is the organ of smell. In Hebrew the same word means both nose and anger, since the flaring nostril was the visible sign of wrath, and that connection governs much of the Old Testament’s language about God.
biblical_def: The Hebrew aph means nose, nostril, and anger, and the double sense lies under a great deal of biblical language. Proverbs states the physical fact and then draws the moral: Surely the churning of milk bringeth forth butter, and the wringing of the nose bringeth forth blood: so the forcing of wrath bringeth forth strife (Proverbs 30:33) — three pressures, three inevitable results, and the third is the one being warned against. The nose appears among the ornaments Isaiah strips from the daughters of Zion: The rings, and nose jewels (Isaiah 3:21). It supplies an image of the strength of behemoth, whom no man traps: He taketh it with his eyes: his nose pierceth through snares (Job 40:24). And the Song uses it in a compliment that startles modern readers: thy nose is as the tower of Lebanon which looketh toward Damascus (Song of Solomon 7:4) — the praise is of a bearing that is upright, watchful and unafraid, not of a shape.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines NOSE as the prominent part of the face which is the organ of smell, consisting of two cavities called nostrils; also the end or snout of anything.
webster_full: NOSE, n. — The prominent part of the face which is the organ of smell, consisting of two cavities called nostrils.
The end of anything; the snout or extremity; as the nose of a bellows.
Scent; sagacity; as a dog with a good nose.
TO LEAD BY THE NOSE, to lead blindly; to cause to follow implicitly.
Anglo-Saxon nosu; Latin nasus; the Hebrew aph means both nostril and anger.
scriptures: Surely the churning of milk bringeth forth butter, and the wringing of the nose bringeth forth blood: so the forcing of wrath bringeth forth strife.
He taketh it with his eyes: his nose pierceth through snares.
Thy neck is as a tower of ivory; thine eyes like the fishpools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bathrabbim: thy nose is as the tower of Lebanon which looketh toward Damascus.
corruption_summary: Because Hebrew uses one word for nose and for anger, the Old Testament’s language about God’s wrath is bodily and vivid, and it is precisely this that modern discomfort with divine wrath tries to explain away.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrew aph is the nostril, and by the obvious physical association it is also anger — the phrase rendered slow to anger (Psalm 103:8; Nahum 1:3) is literally long of nostril, and the fierceness of his anger is a burning nose. This bodily vocabulary is one of the reasons modern readers find the Old Testament’s wrath language uncomfortable, and it is often handled by declaring such expressions mere anthropomorphism, a concession to primitive minds, behind which lies a God who is not really angry at all. That move costs more than it saves. Wrath in Scripture is not a divine mood but God’s settled and holy opposition to sin, and without it the cross has nothing to accomplish — propitiation means the turning away of wrath (Romans 3:25; 1 John 4:10). The figures are accommodation to our capacity, as Calvin taught; what they express is real.

Proverbs 30:33 is a small masterpiece of practical wisdom. Churn milk and you get butter; wring a nose and you get blood; force wrath and you get strife. The middle image is deliberately crude and physical, so that the third cannot be treated as an accident. Strife does not merely happen; it is produced, by pressure applied, and someone applies it. The verse is a rebuke to the common account of quarrels in which no one is responsible and matters simply escalated. James asks the same question and gives the same answer: whence come wars and fightings? They come of the lusts that war in the members (James 4:1).
roots_summary: Hebrew aph (H639), nostril, nose, and by extension anger; nezem (H5141), a ring, worn in the nose or ear; mits (H4330), a pressing or wringing.
roots_lines: Hebrew aph (H639) — the nostril, and so anger; slow to anger is literally long of nostril (Psalm 103:8).
Hebrew mits (H4330) — a squeezing or wringing; the threefold pressure of Proverbs 30:33.
Hebrew nezem (H5141) — a ring worn in the nose or ear; the nose jewels of Isaiah 3:21.
Hebrew appayim — the dual of aph, the two nostrils; the form behind the idiom for patience (Nahum 1:3).
Greek hilasmos (G2434) — propitiation, the turning away of wrath; the New Testament answer to aph.
usage: The wringing of the nose bringeth forth blood: so the forcing of wrath bringeth forth strife (Proverbs 30:33) — strife is produced, not accidental.
His nose pierceth through snares (Job 40:24) — the creature no man traps.
Thy nose is as the tower of Lebanon (Song of Solomon 7:4) — praise of a bearing, upright and watchful.
